Explore On-Time Delivery Charts

Meridian Outfitters: interpreting process performance and variation

How to explore: Review each chart, think about the question, then select Flip to Description to reveal an accessible interpretation. Each card can be opened or closed independently.

Chart 1 of 3

Baseline vs. Current-State

Consider: What changed in average on-time delivery and the spread of the results?

Flip to Description — Chart 1

Bar chart: Average on-time delivery decreases from 96.2% at baseline to 86.0% in the current state.

Histograms: Baseline observations cluster near 96%, while current-state observations spread more broadly around 86%.

Boxplot: Baseline results are higher and more tightly grouped, with an outlier near 80%. Current-state results are generally lower and more variable.

Run chart: Values are mostly in the mid-to-high 90s during baseline, then move into a lower range during the current-state period.

Interpretation: These views show a decline and a change in variation, but do not establish the cause.

Chart 2 of 3

Process Shift: Days 1–30

Consider: Where did the process shift, and what happened to the center line?

Flip to Description — Chart 2

Days 1–20: Mean 95.95%, upper control limit (UCL) 98.23%, lower control limit (LCL) 93.67%. Most readings are near 96%.

Days 21–30: Mean 83.90%, UCL 86.88%, LCL 80.92%. Readings cluster near 84%.

Interpretation: On-time delivery drops sharply between days 20 and 21, suggesting a process shift that should be investigated. The chart shows separate reference lines for the two periods; it does not identify what caused the shift.

Chart 3 of 3

I-Control Chart: Signals to Investigate

Consider: Which data points signal variation that warrants investigation?

Flip to Description — Chart 3

Reference lines: Mean 89.67%, UCL 103.28%, LCL 76.05%.

Data points: Earlier readings are mostly in the mid-to-high 90s. Later readings drop and fluctuate more widely, with several red points below the LCL, including readings near 75%, 70%, and 60%.

Interpretation: A point beyond a control limit is a special-cause signal. These low points warrant investigation. The chart does not identify the root cause by itself.

Other signals discussed in the lesson include nine consecutive points on one side of the center line, six consecutive increases or decreases, and fourteen points alternating up and down.

Key takeaway: A control chart can show a shift, unusual points, or patterns indicating special-cause variation. These signals help teams decide when investigation is needed, but the chart alone cannot prove a root cause.
